title: Constant-distortion Steiner point removal
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every finite connected undirected graph \(G\) with nonnegative real edge lengths and every terminal set \(K\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|K|\geq2\), there is a reweighted terminal-preserving minor \(H\) with vertex set exactly \(K\) satisfying \[d_G(s,t)\leq d_H(s,t)\leq C\,d_G(s,t)\qquad(s,t\in K)?\]
why: Steiner point removal asks how much of a network’s geometry and topology can survive when only designated terminals remain. A universal constant would establish a strong form of graph compression; an unbounded lower bound would show that the topology of general graphs forces a growing loss even when edge lengths may be redesigned.
status_note: The checked 2024 source settles fixed-minor-free graphs and records logarithmic distortion for general graphs. A bounded review on 13 September 2026 did not find a universal constant for all graphs or a refutation. The solved planar question is not presented as still open.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 13 September 2026; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Gupta establishes constant-distortion removal on trees, as recounted in the source’s historical overview.
Filtser gives logarithmic distortion in the terminal count for arbitrary graphs.
Chang and coauthors settle the fixed-minor-free case, including planar graphs; their constant depends on the excluded minor.

sentences: Steiner point removal starts with a weighted graph and a designated set of terminals whose mutual distances matter.
The goal is to delete the other vertices through graph-minor operations, leaving a graph on exactly those terminals.
Its edges may be reweighted, but terminal distances should never shrink and should grow by at most a universal factor.
The same guarantee must work regardless of how many terminals the input contains.
This asks whether graph topology and useful terminal geometry can both survive an extreme reduction in representation size.

definitions: The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_G\) is the minimum path length between its endpoints. Zero-length edges are allowed, so distinct terminals can have distance zero; the displayed inequalities then require their distance in \(H\) to be zero too. To specify precisely the terminal-preserving minor condition, choose pairwise disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets \(B_t\subseteq V(G)\), one for each \(t\in K\), with \(B_t\cap K=\{t\}\). The graph \(H\) is a simple graph on the labeled set \(K\); an edge \(st\) of \(H\) is permitted only if some edge of \(G\) joins \(B_s\) to \(B_t\). Not all such permitted edges have to be kept, and vertices outside the branch sets may be deleted. Thus vertices can be deleted, edges deleted or contracted, and parallel edges or loops removed, but no two terminals are identified and no surviving vertex is a nonterminal. Each edge of \(H\) may receive an arbitrary new nonnegative real length, independent of the original length of an edge witnessing its adjacency. This is a topological minor relation with allowed reweighting, not a requirement that contraction preserve inherited edge lengths. Define \(d_H\) by shortest paths and as infinity for disconnected pairs; the guarantee forces finite terminal distances. Both inequalities must hold simultaneously for all pairs in one chosen minor. The same \(C\) must work independently of the numbers of vertices, edges and terminals, graph topology, edge-length magnitudes and aspect ratio. The target is existential and imposes no construction-time, input-encoding or randomness requirement on a proof of existence.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a universal constant and the required rooted minor for every input in Lean, or prove its negation: for every finite \(C\), some graph and terminal set admit no minor meeting all the inequalities. A family with unbounded necessary distortion is a valid negative answer; a single fixed lower bound on the constant is not. Expected distortion for each pair, additional surviving Steiner vertices, or a guarantee only in a restricted graph class does not settle the statement.

context_blocks.text: The source describes Steiner point removal for general graphs before solving the version excluding a fixed graph minor. This card retains the general-graph question from the inherited record. The word minor includes terminal identities and permitted edge reweighting, which are made explicit in the branch-set definition.

Filtser obtains distortion \(O(\log k)\) for arbitrary graphs with \(k\) terminals. This bounds the loss in terms of the size of the surviving vertex set, but does not provide a constant independent of that size.

For trees, the source recounts an upper bound of eight and examples with necessary distortion approaching eight. Thus even on trees exact preservation is not generally possible, and a universal positive answer must allow nontrivial distortion.

Chang, Conroy, Le, Milenković, Solomon and Than prove constant distortion for every class excluding a fixed complete graph minor. More specifically, for \(K_r\)-minor-free graphs their Theorem 1.4 gives \(2^{O(r\log r)}\) distortion. This settles the planar case and much more, but the constant depends on the excluded minor and is not uniform over all graphs.

If the minor condition is dropped, the complete graph on the terminals with original shortest-path distances as edge lengths preserves every terminal distance exactly. The scientific constraint is preserving a graph-minor representation while removing every other vertex. Distances alone would give a much easier problem.

Choosing a distribution over minors with a small expected stretch for each pair need not produce a single minor that has small stretch on every pair. Likewise, allowing a few extra vertices changes the compression target. Neither relaxation is silently included here.
